exam: A 35‑year‑old man with new‑onset nephrotic syndrome and microscopic hematuria – what is the next best step and why? — Biopsy to differentiate minimal change from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, which changes steroid strategy.
You are about to biopsy a patient with eGFR 12 mL/min/1.73 m² – how do you proceed? — Optimize coagulation, consider dialysis access, discuss risk‑benefit; if unsafe, seek alternative diagnosis.

Post‑biopsy ultrasound shows a 3 cm perinephric hematoma but the patient is stable – what management is appropriate? — Continue observation, serial hemoglobin, analgesia; intervene only if size increases or hemodynamics worsen.
Biopsy reveals pauci‑immune crescentic GN – which serology should you order and what treatment follows? — Order ANCA; start high‑dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab, avoid NSAIDs.

In a resource‑limited hospital without immunofluorescence, how can you still reach a diagnosis in suspected lupus nephritis? — Use clinical criteria, serology (ANA, anti‑dsDNA), and light‑microscopy patterns (wire loops, full‑house staining) to guide therapy.

A patient develops gross hematuria 4 hours after biopsy – what immediate actions are required? — Stop any anticoagulants, place Foley catheter, obtain urgent ultrasound, prepare for possible embolisation or transfusion.
Why is hypertension control essential before kidney biopsy? — High pressure increases risk of arterial puncture and bleeding; target <140/90 mmHg before the procedure.

What are the histological features that distinguish membranous nephropathy from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis? — Membranous shows subepithelial immune deposits and thickened GBM; FSGS shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis without immune deposits.
ai.title: Kidney Biopsy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Kidney biopsy provides tissue diagnosis for renal disease, guiding treatment and prognosis. In low‑resource settings, indications, technique, and interpretation must be adapted to available tools.

b: Usually performed percutaneously under local anaesthesia
Ultrasound guidance is preferred; blind technique may be used where imaging is unavailable
Specimens are processed for light microscopy, immunofluorescence and, when possible, electron microscopy
sections.p: Kidney biopsy obtains a core of renal cortex for histopathology. It is the definitive test when clinical and laboratory data cannot distinguish glomerular, tubulointerstitial, vascular, or hereditary kidney disease.

b: Indications: unexplained nephrotic syndrome in adults, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, atypical hematuria, renal masses, transplant dysfunction
Contraindications: uncontrolled hypertension (>180/110 mmHg), bleeding diathesis, solitary kidney with poor function, active infection at puncture site
Complications: bleeding (hematoma, gross hematuria), arteriovenous fistula, pain, infection
sections.p: Understanding when and how to biopsy prevents unnecessary risk and ensures the result will change management.

b: In nephrotic syndrome, distinguishes minimal change disease (steroid‑responsive) from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (poor response)
In rapidly progressive GN, identifies pauci‑immune (ANCA‑associated), immune‑complex (lupus, post‑infectious) or anti‑GBM disease, each with specific treatment
In transplant patients, detects acute rejection versus drug toxicity
sections.p: Kidney biopsy directly influences therapeutic choices, especially immunosuppression, and provides prognostic information.

t.b: Is the patient safe to undergo a percutaneous procedure? Normal PT/INR <1.5, platelets >100 ×10⁹/L allow biopsy; correct abnormalities first
Can the kidney be visualised and is there a safe window? Identifies cysts, hydronephrosis, or solitary kidney; if unavailable, a blind approach is possible but higher risk
Is renal function sufficient to tolerate a biopsy? eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² raises risk; consider alternative diagnosis or transplant biopsy
What pattern of injury is suggested? RBC casts point to glomerular disease; heavy proteinuria suggests nephrotic syndrome

b: If histology shows immune‑mediated GN, start high‑dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab; avoid NSAIDs which worsen renal injury
For minimal change disease, give oral prednisolone; avoid calcineurin inhibitors unless steroid‑resistant
Supportive care: control blood pressure (ACE‑I/ARB), manage edema (loop diuretics), treat anemia, monitor electrolytes
If bleeding occurs, apply pressure, give tranexamic acid, and arrange urgent imaging; transfuse if hemodynamically unstable
sections.p: After a biopsy, treat the underlying pathology and monitor for complications.

b: Skipping coagulation checks leads to preventable hematoma
Assuming a normal ultrasound excludes all risks; small vessels may still bleed
Over‑reliance on light microscopy without immunofluorescence can miss lupus or IgA nephropathy
Delaying treatment while awaiting biopsy in rapidly progressive GN can cause irreversible loss
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from inadequate preparation or misinterpretation of pathology.

Identify complications that require urgent imaging

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden flank pain with expanding hematoma after biopsy
Gross hematuria with drop in hemoglobin >2 g/dL
Signs of infection at puncture site (fever, redness, swelling)
